title: Jeremiah 42:1–6
context: After Ishmael’s murder of Gedaliah (chapters 40–41), Johanan son of Kareah, the other captains, and all the people come to Jeremiah. They ask him to pray to the LORD for the remnant and to tell them what they should do, and they swear before the LORD to obey whatever he says, good or bad. Jeremiah agrees to pray and to keep nothing back. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about seeking God in prayer and the weight of promises made before him.

verses.text: Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even to the greatest, came near,
verses.arminianNotes:
The captains, Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people, least to greatest, approach Jeremiah. The survivors of Gedaliah’s murder seek guidance.

Arminian readers see a community at a crossroads, facing a real choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The setting follows chapters 40–41, where Gedaliah was killed and the people gathered near Bethlehem intending to go to Egypt (41:17–18).

Reformed readers see God’s people under pressure seeking a word. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: and said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Please let our supplication be presented before you, and pray for us to the LORD your God, even for all this remnant, for we are left but a few of many, as your eyes see us,
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask Jeremiah to present their plea and pray to the LORD his God for the remnant, few out of many. They ask for intercession.

Arminian readers see a genuine request for prayer (compare the box at Joshua 10:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
They speak of “the LORD your God,” a phrasing that may hint at distance, though it may simply be respectful.

Reformed readers see prayer as the right first step in crisis. Both traditions read this as shared ground about seeking God through prayer.

verses.text: that the LORD your God may show us the way in which we should walk, and the things that we should do.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask that the LORD show them the way to walk and the things to do. They seek direction.

Arminian readers see a request that, if sincere, opens the way for real guidance and real obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The request is right in itself; the following chapters show whether their hearts matched their words.

Reformed readers see the proper desire to know God’s will. Both traditions read this as shared ground about seeking God’s guidance before acting, while the narrative will test their sincerity.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah the prophet said to them, “I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your words; and it will happen that whatever thing the LORD answers you, I will declare it to you. I will keep nothing back from you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah agrees to pray to the LORD their God as they asked, and to tell them everything the LORD answers, keeping nothing back. The prophet commits to faithfulness.

Arminian readers see a prophet willing to serve even those likely to resist.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah’s “the LORD your God” returns their own phrase to them.

Reformed readers see a faithful messenger who will not alter God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithful intercession and honest reporting of what God says.

verses.text: Then they said to Jeremiah, “May the LORD be a true and faithful witness among us, if we don’t do according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to tell us.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people call on the LORD as a true and faithful witness against them if they fail to do all he says through Jeremiah. They bind themselves by oath.

Arminian readers see a solemn, freely made commitment.
verses.reformedNotes:
The oath sets a standard by which their later actions will be judged (42:20).

Reformed readers see the seriousness of vows made before God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about integrity in speech and the weight of promises made in God’s name.

verses.text: Whether it is good, or whether it is bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God, to whom we send you; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of the LORD our God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They promise to obey the LORD’s voice whether the answer is good or bad, so that it may go well with them. Their pledge is complete.

Arminian readers see a sincere-sounding commitment whose test lies ahead.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise of obedience “whether it is good, or whether it is bad” will be tested when the answer contradicts their plans.

Reformed readers see how easily the heart promises more than it performs. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
